report:
## Conclusion

**Arthroscopy does not provide meaningful benefit for knee osteoarthritis and is not recommended for most patients.**

Multiple high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines consistently show that arthroscopic surgery (including lavage, debridement, and partial meniscectomy) is **no more effective than placebo surgery or conservative (non-surgical) treatment** for knee osteoarthritis.

### Key Evidence:

1. **Landmark RCT (NEJM, 2002):** Moseley et al. conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial and found that arthroscopic surgery was no better than sham (placebo) surgery in relieving pain or improving function in patients with osteoarthritis of the knee. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259))

2. **Cochrane Review (2022):** A comprehensive Cochrane review assessed arthroscopic surgery versus placebo or non-surgical treatment for degenerative knee disease and found no clinically meaningful benefit. ([https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease))

3. **Recent Meta-analysis (2024):** A systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that arthroscopic surgery is not superior to conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis. ([https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3))

4. **Clinical Practice Guideline:** An international panel strongly recommended **against** arthroscopic knee surgery in patients with degenerative knee disease, noting that financial and other incentives may explain why the procedure remains common despite evidence against its use. ([https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline))

### Bottom Line:
For the vast majority of patients with knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopy offers no benefit over conservative treatments such as physical therapy, exercise, weight management, and medications. Some surgeons argue it may help a select subgroup with mild OA and specific mechanical issues (e.g., a locked knee from a meniscal tear), but the overall evidence strongly discourages routine use. Patients should discuss conservative management options with their physician before considering arthroscopy.
